The Enterprise Test Plan consisted of three different solvent campaigns. The first campaign was an MEA campaign, which was made up of some final commissioning activities and a short parametric testing period to baseline the system with an industry standard solvent. Subsequently, ION completed an ICE-21™ and then an ICE-31® campaign. Both the ICE-21™ and ICE-31® campaigns had a period of parametric testing followed by a longer-term steady-state operating period. The long-term testing of ICE-31® was substantially longer than the prior tests to allow for more in-depth analysis of the performance of aged ICE-31® solvent. This type of investigation was not included in the MEA and ICE-21™ campaigns and thus the testing periods could be compressed. The baseline comparison was based on parametric testing data and was thus independent of the length of each solvent campaign. A Gantt chart of the test plan is shown in Figure 7-1. Figure 7-1: Enterprise Test Plan 7.1 Work Package 1 – MEA 7.1.1 Baseline In the first Work Package (WP), the objective was to develop a baseline for MEA performance on the ENTP system by finding the highest capture efficiency. Flue gas flow and temperature were held constant at standard conditions (~14,500 lb/hr at 96 °F). Stripper pressure was also held constant. Solvent flow rate varied along with the cold-rich bypass ratio. Stripper steam flow was held constant; thus, stripper sump temperature varied slightly with changing solvent flow rates. Capture efficiency and SRD varied with changing flow rate as well. Due to foaming during the MEA campaign, the system was unstable, resulting in fluctuating L/G ratios that made it difficult to control the capture efficiency and resulting SRDs. Absorber column capacity was also impacted, which limited high L/G cases at the design flue gas flow. ION Clean Energy 17 DE-FE0031950: FINAL PROJECT REPORT 7.1.2 Flue Gas Turndown ION operated the system with varying flue gas flow rates. Flue gas temperature was held constant, as was solvent flow rate, cold-rich bypass ratio, and stripper pressure. Stripper sump temperature varied slightly. The capture efficiency and SRD varied as dependent variables. The objective was to evaluate turndown performance with MEA. In theory, maintaining solvent flow rate and steam flow constant while reducing flue gas flow rate will result in a measurable increase in capture efficiency and SRD. Regenerator column capacity was limited due to the foaming, which prevented high capture efficiency cases. 7.2 Work Package 2 – ICE-21™ 7.2.1 Baseline The flue gas flow rate and temperature were held constant.
